## Tonight's question {.title-slide data-background-color="#102a43"}

::: {.hero-statement}
How do people and HR practices help an organization accomplish its mission?
:::

::: {.hero-question}
Strategic alignment, workforce planning, and succession planning
:::

## A workforce challenge {.activity-slide data-background-color="#176b87"}

::: {.activity-prompt}
Think of a government or nonprofit organization you know. What workforce problem makes its mission harder to achieve?
:::

- What work suffers? 
- What would a manager need to know before responding?

::: {.activity-close}
Five minutes in groups. Put it on the white board.
:::

<aside class="notes">Write each group's problem on the board under "Tonight's problems" and leave it up. Reuse them on the alignment, gaps-and-surpluses, succession, and measures slides, and in the closing activity. Define a workforce challenge or give an example if the room stalls. Connect to Chapter 1: human capital includes knowledge, skills, abilities, and competencies. About six minutes including the round.</aside>

## Strategic human resource management

HR decisions connect the organization's people and capabilities to its goals.

::: {.incremental}
- What does the organization need to accomplish?
- What capabilities will that require?
- How will HR practices develop and support those capabilities?
- What evidence will show whether the approach works?
:::

::: {.takeaway .fragment}
People are an asset to develop, not a cost to minimize. Strategic HRM moves from managing positions to managing talent.
:::

<aside class="notes">Source: author slides 5 and 7; instructor manual p. 17. Strategic HRM is an ongoing approach to managing people. Workforce planning is one way to put that approach into practice. Plant the takeaway line now: Urbanopolis after the break is a budget process that treats people as a cost line. Ask students to watch for where Pat can still act as if people are the asset.</aside>

## HR's role in organizational decisions

::: {.compare .roomy}
<div class="compare-side"><span class="card-heading">Transactional</span>

Accurate pay, benefits, records, and dependable employment processes

</div>
<div class="compare-side"><span class="card-heading">Transformational</span>

A seat at the table: advice about staffing capacity, employee development, and whether organizational goals are feasible

</div>
:::

::: {.takeaway .fragment}
Strategic HRM depends on reliable administration and a voice in setting direction.
:::

::: {.question-bar .fragment}
Where you work: is HR asked before a commitment is made, or after?
:::

<aside class="notes">Source: author slide 7 and its notes, instructor manual p. 17 (transactional and transformational components). Take two or three answers to the question on the slide; ask what happened when HR came in after the commitment. Avoid treating transactional work as unimportant.</aside>

## A service goal with conflicting incentives

::: {.scenario}
<span class="card-heading">Hypothetical: a benefits office</span>

The office wants residents to receive accurate eligibility decisions sooner.

Managers reward staff for closing more cases each day. Training time reduces that daily count.
:::

::: {.big-question .fragment}
What behavior does this system encourage?
:::

<aside class="notes">Instructor-created hypothetical applying author slide 9. Ask whether speed alone captures the mission. Probe for errors, repeat contacts, appeals, staff learning, and access. Do not supply an answer before students diagnose the mismatch.</aside>

## What a strategic approach can offer

::: {.compare .roomy}
<div class="compare-side"><span class="card-heading">For employees</span>

A clearer connection between their work and the mission, useful feedback, and support for development

</div>
<div class="compare-side"><span class="card-heading">For managers</span>

Evidence for resource decisions and a way to assess whether new commitments fit existing capacity

</div>
:::

::: {.takeaway .fragment}
Strategy also means knowing what not to do. Would an attractive new grant make the organization less able to deliver what it already promises?
:::

<aside class="notes">Source: author slide 10 and its notes (Porter on strategy as knowing what not to do). These are potential benefits, not guaranteed effects. Introduce mission creep as taking on work that diverts capacity from core purposes; the takeaway question is the manual's grant example.</aside>

## Workforce planning {.section-slide data-background-color="#102a43"}

<aside class="notes">Source: author slide 11. Transition from the strategic approach to a concrete planning process.</aside>

## The workforce planning process

::: {.lead-in}
Five steps, cyclical
:::

::: {.pathway .wp-path}
<div class="pathway-step fragment"><span class="card-heading">1 · Direction</span><p>What must we accomplish?</p></div>
<div class="pathway-arrow fragment">→</div>
<div class="pathway-step fragment"><span class="card-heading">2 · Analysis</span><p>What workforce do we have, and what do we need?</p></div>
<div class="pathway-arrow fragment">→</div>
<div class="pathway-step fragment"><span class="card-heading">3 · Action plan</span><p>How will we close the gaps?</p></div>
<div class="pathway-arrow fragment">→</div>
<div class="pathway-step fragment"><span class="card-heading">4 · Implement</span><p>Who is responsible for each action, by when?</p></div>
<div class="pathway-arrow fragment">→</div>
<div class="pathway-step fragment"><span class="card-heading">5 · Evaluate</span><p>Did it work? What needs revising?</p></div>
:::

::: {.takeaway .fragment}
Discovering a workforce constraint may send you back to the goal, the budget, or the timeline.
:::

<aside class="notes">Source: author slide 12. Present this as an iterative process. The strip at the top of the next slides shows where we are in it.</aside>

## Strategic direction and the HR audit

::: {.wp-track}
<span class="wp-step is-current">1 Direction</span><span class="wp-step">2 Analysis</span><span class="wp-step">3 Action plan</span><span class="wp-step">4 Implement</span><span class="wp-step">5 Evaluate</span>
:::

**Direction:** What must the organization accomplish now and over the next several years?

**HR audit:** What do existing policies, practices, and workforce information reveal about its ability to do that work?

::: {.incremental}
- Review roles, staffing, compensation, and performance processes.
- Identify what works and where capacity or information is missing.
:::

<aside class="notes">Source: author slide 13 and instructor manual p. 18. Explain that an HR audit is a structured assessment, not simply an employee count. It can expose outdated job descriptions, inconsistent practices, or missing information. No legal compliance determination is being made here.</aside>

## Activity: the staffing implications of a goal {.activity-slide data-background-color="#176b87"}

::: {.activity-prompt}
Hypothetical: a city will open its permit counter two evenings each week using its existing staffing budget.
:::

1. What work and skills will evening service require?
2. What do you need to learn about the current workforce?
3. Are there any tradeoffs  leadership resolve should before promising this service?

[**Think about the potential varying perspectives :** HR director · budget analyst · counter supervisor · resident who works days]{.activity-roles}

::: {.activity-close}
Five minutes in groups.
:::

<aside class="notes">Instructor-created hypothetical adapting author slide 14's strategic-goal exercise. Assign one role per group (four groups of three). Allow about eight minutes including reports. The roles should produce disagreement: HR sees training and supervision; Budget sees the flat budget; the supervisor sees daytime coverage and burnout; the resident sees access. Listen for scheduling, supervision, IT support, training, workload, and effects on daytime service. Keep the focus on translating a goal into workforce requirements.</aside>

## The workforce we have and the workforce we need

::: {.wp-track}
<span class="wp-step">1 Direction</span><span class="wp-step is-current">2 Analysis</span><span class="wp-step">3 Action plan</span><span class="wp-step">4 Implement</span><span class="wp-step">5 Evaluate</span>
:::

::: {.table-block .roomy}

| Current workforce | Future requirements |
|---|---|
| Knowledge, Skills, Abilities | Work needed to meet service goals |
| Career stage and anticipated departures | Capabilities that may disappear |
| Hours, positions, and funding sources | Sustainable staffing and funding |
| Current workload and constraints | Gaps, surpluses, or work to redesign |
| Rules, contracts, and required staffing levels | Constraints any plan must respect |

:::

<aside class="notes">Source: author slide 15, including its line on external constraints or rules (accreditation, safety staffing). The constraints row sets up Urbanopolis: budget instructions that allow only supervisory cuts, deleted classifications, and pending union negotiations. Distinguish headcount, funded positions, and full-time equivalents. Two half-time employees can equal one FTE. Avoid treating demographic categories as proxies for an individual's abilities or retirement plans. Gather evidence about actual skills and likely departures.</aside>

## Responses to gaps and surpluses

::: {.wp-track}
<span class="wp-step">1 Direction</span><span class="wp-step">2 Analysis</span><span class="wp-step is-current">3 Action plan</span><span class="wp-step">4 Implement</span><span class="wp-step">5 Evaluate</span>
:::

::: {.compare .roomy}
<div class="compare-side"><span class="card-heading">A capability gap</span>

Recruit, develop current employees, redesign work, or reconsider the service commitment.

</div>
<div class="compare-side"><span class="card-heading">A surplus in some work</span>

Consider redeployment, retraining, attrition, or position reductions in light of service needs.

</div>
:::

::: {.takeaway .fragment}
An organization can have a surplus in one role/position and a shortage in another.
:::

<aside class="notes">Sources: author slide 16, instructor manual p. 20 workforce-planning definition and discussion of gaps and surpluses. Options here are illustrative and depend on authority, rules, costs, and timing. Ask students to return to the permit-counter example, or a problem on the board: what could they do immediately, and what would require time or approval?</aside>

## Succession planning

::: {.wp-track}
<span class="wp-step">1 Direction</span><span class="wp-step">2 Analysis</span><span class="wp-step is-current">3 Action plan</span><span class="wp-step">4 Implement</span><span class="wp-step">5 Evaluate</span>
:::

Which departures would put essential work at risk?

- Identify key leadership and service positions.
- Identify the competencies future employees will need.
- Develop internal capability and consider external recruitment.
- Prepare for an unexpected vacancy as well as a planned transition.

<aside class="notes">Sources: author slides 17–19 and instructor manual p. 20. A critical position can be a specialist or frontline role. Succession planning includes knowledge transfer and development. It should not imply a guaranteed promotion for a chosen successor. Ask whether any problem on the board is really a succession problem.</aside>

## A vacancy beyond the leadership team

::: {.scenario}
<span class="card-heading">Hypothetical: one experienced analyst</span>

Only one analyst knows how to produce a required monthly report. The report draws on several systems, and the process lives mostly in the analyst's memory.
:::

::: {.question-bar .fragment}
Show of hands: are you the only person at work who knows how to do something?
:::

::: {.big-question .fragment}
What should the manager do before that person leaves?
:::

<aside class="notes">Instructor-created hypothetical applying author slides 18–19. Take the show of hands first; ask one or two people what the thing is and what happens when they take a week off. Then the question. Listen for documentation, cross-training, protected learning time, and backup responsibility. Probe: who has time to learn? How would you know the backup can actually complete the work? Keep to roughly three minutes.</aside>

## Implementation and evidence

::: {.wp-track}
<span class="wp-step">1 Direction</span><span class="wp-step">2 Analysis</span><span class="wp-step">3 Action plan</span><span class="wp-step is-current">4 Implement</span><span class="wp-step is-current">5 Evaluate</span>
:::

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="38%"}
A plan needs an owner, resources, and a timeline.

- Assign responsibility for each action.
- Agree on measures and review dates.
- Discuss progress in regular management meetings.
- Adjust when results or service needs change.
:::
::: {.column width="62%"}
::: {.table-block}

| Management question | Possible evidence |
|---|---|
| Can we fill needed roles? | Vacancy duration, qualified applicant pools |
| Can staff perform the work? | Demonstrated competencies, error rates |
| Is service improving? | Timeliness, accuracy, differences across users |
| Can we sustain it? | Turnover, workload, employee feedback |

:::
:::
::::

::: {.question-bar .fragment}
Pick one problem from the board(s). What measure would provide evidence about whether it's improving?
:::

<aside class="notes">Sources: author slide 20, including the implementation SmartArt, and instructor-created measures applying author slides 6, 9, and 20. Emphasize feasibility: a training plan without time for employees to attend is incomplete. Measures describe possible evidence, not established causal relationships. Two minutes on the closing question: take one measure per group, and ask what comparison or baseline would be needed. If errors rise, consider changes in case complexity or systems alongside workforce explanations.</aside>

## What would you tell your manager? {.activity-slide data-background-color="#176b87"}

::: {.activity-prompt}
Return to the workforce problem your group put on the board.
:::

- What organizational goal is at stake?
- What evidence would you gather first?
- What HR decision might that evidence change?

<aside class="notes">Sources: author slides 21–22 and instructor manual pp. 20–21. Leave roughly four minutes. Ask for one changed answer from the opening discussion. Reinforce the link between the mission, workforce capabilities, and evidence.</aside>

## Two mindsets for strategic HRM

::: {.compare .roomy}
<div class="compare-side"><span class="card-heading">Growth</span>

Hire, develop, and expand. Most of the chapter, and most of what the field teaches, assumes an organization that is adding capacity.

</div>
<div class="compare-side accent"><span class="card-heading">Austerity</span>

Cut, consolidate, and reduce in force. The reality for many public and nonprofit organizations, and the harder test of whether people are treated as an asset.

</div>
:::

::: {.takeaway .fragment}
Tonight's case is strategic HRM under austerity. What can Pat Alvarez do?
:::

<aside class="notes">Source: instructor manual p. 21, which recommends Urbanopolis because SHRM is usually taught "with a growth mindset" while most organizations face fiscal austerity. Say the line, then break. Pat has to cut 8.5% from a budget that is 97% people, write the citywide RIF rules, and fill a Council-priority vacancy at the same time.</aside>
